strataMetadata.label: SS 1 Literature in English — Complete Question Set (200 Questions)

questions.text: Who is the playwright of the dramatic text 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Femi Osofisan
Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan
Wole Soyinka
Ola Rotimi
questions.explanation: 'Once Upon an Elephant' was written by the Nigerian dramatist and scholar Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan.

questions.text: What is the birth name of the usurper king, Ajanaku, before he assumed the throne?
options: Odejimi
Olaniyonu
Odekunle
Akinjobi
questions.explanation: Before assuming the monarchical praise-name Ajanaku, the character is personally named Olaniyonu.

questions.text: Who is the legitimate reigning monarch whose mysterious affliction creates the leadership vacuum exploited by conspirators?
options: Oba Ogundele
Oba Akinjobi
Oba Ajasa
Oba Odejimi
questions.explanation: Oba Akinjobi is the legitimate king incapacitated by a mysterious ailment engineered by palace conspirators.

questions.text: What specific role does Serubawon occupy in the traditional administration of the kingdom?
options: The Chief Priest of Ogun
The Chief Kingmaker and senior council member
The Captain of the Royal Guards
The Palace Praise-singer
questions.explanation: Serubawon is the influential chief kingmaker whose political machinations subvert traditional succession.

questions.text: Which sacred traditional coronation rites does Serubawon fraudulently perform to enthrone Ajanaku?
options: The Ijedodo ritual
The Olubori rites
The Oro rites
The Agemo ceremonies
questions.explanation: Serubawon manipulates traditional protocols by performing the sacred Olubori rites to crown Olaniyonu as king.

questions.text: Who is the steadfast chief that openly and repeatedly opposes the fraudulent enthronement of Ajanaku?
options: Ajasa
Odejimi
Serubawon
Ogundele
questions.explanation: Chief Odejimi steadfastly refuses to compromise, standing for traditional legitimacy and moral integrity.

questions.text: Who is the wife of Chief Odejimi and mother to Odekunle?
options: Demoke
Iyale
Omoyeni
Desola
questions.explanation: Iyale is the devoted wife of Chief Odejimi and mother to Odekunle.

questions.text: Who is the wife of Serubawon and mother of Desola?
options: Iyale
Demoke
Omoyeni
Yosola
questions.explanation: Demoke is the wife of Serubawon and was also instrumental in past palace intrigues.

questions.text: Who is Iya Agba within the royal and historical framework of the kingdom?
options: The market queen mother
The senior queen and eldest wife of the former monarch
The chief priestess of the earth shrine
Serubawon's estranged sister
questions.explanation: Iya Agba is the venerable senior queen of the late king, possessing deep memory of ancestral customs.

questions.text: What malicious allegation did Serubawon and Demoke orchestrate against Iya Agba years before the play's main action?
options: Stealing palace treasures
Adultery and infidelity to the king
Practicing witchcraft to kill the royal prince
Poisoning communal wells
questions.explanation: Serubawon and Demoke framed Iya Agba for adultery, resulting in her humiliating expulsion from the royal palace.

questions.text: Who is the young hunter betrothed to Desola?
options: Delani
Odekunle
Dele
Yele
questions.explanation: Odekunle, son of Chief Odejimi and Iyale, is the betrothed lover of Desola.

questions.text: Who was the true betrothed lover of Omoyeni before King Ajanaku forcibly claimed her?
options: Odekunle
Delani
Lere
Odegbami
questions.explanation: Delani had completed bride-service for Omoyeni's father, Ajasa, before Ajanaku used monarchical power to seize her.

questions.text: What is the name of Omoyeni's father, who capitulates to royal pressure?
options: Odejimi
Ajasa
Serubawon
Ogundele
questions.explanation: Ajasa is Omoyeni's father who cowers before royal pressure and yields his daughter to Ajanaku.

questions.text: What dark ritual does King Ajanaku pursue to secure absolute power and physical immortality?
options: The Olubori rites
The Ijedodo ritual
The Ogun cleansing
The Osun festival
questions.explanation: Ajanaku seeks demonic invulnerability and eternal life through the horrific Ijedodo ritual.

questions.text: How many virgins are demanded as victims under the conditions of the Ijedodo ritual?
options: Three
Six
Seven
Twelve
questions.explanation: The dark covenant demands the sexual defilement and spiritual sacrifice of six virgins across ninety days.

questions.text: Who is ambushed on the bush path and becomes the tragic sixth virgin victim?
options: Yosola
Desola
Omoyeni
Iyale
questions.explanation: Desola, Serubawon's only beloved daughter, is seized on the pathway as the final victim.

questions.text: What fatal condition befalls the young women violated in the Ijedodo ritual?
options: They become mute palace handmaidens.
They suffer a wasting illness and gradually die.
They are blinded and cast into the forest.
They are executed immediately in the shrine.
questions.explanation: The ritual siphons their life force, causing them to wither away in agony and die.

questions.text: Who is Desola's trusted companion when she leaves the compound to meet Odekunle?
options: Omoyeni
Yosola
Iyale
Demoke
questions.explanation: Yosola is Desola's trusted confidante who accompanies her on her secret rendezvous.

questions.text: What startling biological truth does Iya Agba reveal about Ajanaku's paternity?
options: He is the legitimate son of late King Akinjobi.
He is Serubawon's illegitimate son from an adulterous affair with Adebisi.
He is an orphan child found in the shrine.
He is the biological son of Chief Odejimi.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba reveals that Serubawon fathered Ajanaku out of wedlock with Adebisi, explaining his desperate scheme to crown him.

questions.text: How many scenes comprise the complete dramatic structure of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Ten scenes
Fourteen scenes
Twelve scenes
Sixteen scenes
questions.explanation: The play unfolds across a unified dramatic arc composed of fourteen sequential scenes.

questions.text: What does the titular 'Elephant' (Ajanaku/Erin) symbolize in the socio-political allegory?
options: Agrarian fertility and rainfall
Heavy, destructive despotism and unbridled political tyranny
Traditional spiritual enlightenment
The commercial wealth of ivory trading
questions.explanation: The elephant represents oppressive autocracy, military dictatorship, and rulers who crush the populace.

questions.text: Which traditional Yoruba trickster archetype does Chief Serubawon personify?
options: The Lion (Kiniun)
The Tortoise (Ijapa)
The Dog (Aja)
The Falcon (Awodi)
questions.explanation: Serubawon embodies Ijapa, the manipulative trickster who orchestrates schemes and lures giants to destruction.

questions.text: Whose celebrated Yoruba oral poem provided key creative inspiration for the dramatist?
options: J.P. Clark's 'Night Rain'
Adeboye Babalola's 'Salute to the Elephant'
Gabriel Okara's 'Piano and Drums'
Wole Soyinka's 'Idanre'
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan was inspired by Adeboye Babalola's celebrated rendition of the Yoruba oral chant 'Salute to the Elephant'.

questions.text: What does the classical Yoruba proverb 'Ajanaku kọja mo ri nkan firi' emphasize in the play?
options: fleeting glimpse is insufficient to comprehend the immense weight of the elephant.
Hunters must never walk in pairs during night hunts.
Small animals must flee whenever large drums are beaten.
The king's crown is crafted from solid gold.
questions.explanation: The proverb denotes that the elephant's towering magnitude commands total, unavoidable attention.

questions.text: What does the folktale song 'Erin karele o wa joba' dramatize when sung by Iya Agba?
options: genuine song of praise for royal valor
The tortoise deceptively luring the elephant to a covered pit with promises of a throne
lullaby sung to royal infants
dirge sung during royal burials
questions.explanation: The chant recalls the myth where the tortoise flatters the proud elephant to walk into a concealed death pit.

questions.text: What does the covered pit draped in luxurious cloth represent allegorically?
options: well-built granary for food storage
The perilous abyss of hubris and deceptive court sycophancy
secret armory built by hunters
sacred ancestral pool
questions.explanation: The disguised pit represents the dangerous trap set by flattery that ensnares conceited rulers.

questions.text: Which hunter alongside Odejimi maintains unwavering integrity against palace corruption?
options: Odegbami
Delani
Yele
Dele
questions.explanation: Odegbami stands as a resolute hunter loyal to custom and opposed to Serubawon's unlawful designs.

questions.text: What is the primary literary genre of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Pastoral romantic comedy
Political satirical drama
Melodramatic domestic farce
Biographical chronicle
questions.explanation: The play is a biting political satire exposing governance decay, autocracy, and societal complicity.

questions.text: How does the play depict the traditional African worldview regarding the relationship between the ruler and the land?
options: The monarch's private conduct has no connection to nature.
wicked or illegitimate ruler brings spiritual defilement, drought, and sickness upon the entire realm.
The gods favor any ruler who possesses the strongest army.
Royal authority supersedes cosmic and natural laws.
questions.explanation: In African cosmologies, the moral rectitude of the sovereign is organically tied to the land's well-being and health.

questions.text: What does the Hunters' Guild represent in the societal structure of the kingdom?
options: commercial meat trading syndicate
The communal defense force, security vanguard, and champions of physical bravery
fringe religious cult without civic duties
Servants dedicated to palace domestic labor
questions.explanation: The hunters form the warrior backbone and defenders of societal boundaries and communal justice.

questions.text: What tragic irony engulfs Chief Serubawon regarding the Ijedodo virgin sacrifice?
options: He loses his palace title before the ritual concludes.
His own daughter Desola becomes the sixth victim of the horrific ritual he helped enable.
The gods turn him into an elephant.
His co-conspirators banish him from the town council.
questions.explanation: In poetic justice, Serubawon's treasured daughter becomes the final sacrificial victim of his tyrannical creation.

questions.text: What is King Ajanaku's principal tragic flaw (hamartia)?
options: Indecisiveness and fear of battle
Uncontrollable hubris, megalomania, and lust for divine immortality
Excessive mercy toward political traitors
Reckless squandering of state wealth on feasts
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is undone by overwhelming pride, intoxication with power, and the delusion of living forever.

questions.text: How does Ajanaku rule on the land dispute brought before him by two peasant women?
options: He grants the land to the poorer woman.
He confiscates the land for the palace and himself.
He orders the elders to divide the parcel equally.
He gives the land to Chief Serubawon.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku displays rapacious greed by appropriating the disputed land for his own personal domain.

questions.text: What does Ajanaku do when emissaries from an afflicted neighboring settlement come pleading for aid?
options: He provides grains from the royal storehouses.
He mocks their misery and imposes steeper tribute requirements upon them.
He deploys the royal guards to defend their boundaries.
He steps down from his throne in sympathy.
questions.explanation: He exhibits callous disdain, rejecting their pleas and demanding further extortionate levies.

questions.text: Whom does Omoyeni name as the true father of the child in her womb?
options: King Ajanaku
Delani
Odekunle
Serubawon
questions.explanation: Omoyeni reveals that her betrothed lover Delani fathered the baby, invalidating Ajanaku's claim.

questions.text: Who provides sanctuary, emotional strength, and traditional midwifery to Omoyeni?
options: Demoke
Iya Agba
Yosola
Serubawon
questions.explanation: Iya Agba shelters Omoyeni in her cottage and safely delivers the child away from palace malice.

questions.text: How does Chief Serubawon die at the climax of the play?
options: He is shot by Odekunle with an enchanted arrow.
He commits suicide after the full revelation of his incestuous and treasonous misdeeds.
He is trampled to death by an actual elephant.
He dies in his sleep of an unknown disease.
questions.explanation: Shattered by guilt, public exposure, and his daughter's violation, Serubawon ends his own life.

questions.text: During which communal festival is Ajanaku's metaphysical power neutralized?
options: The New Yam Festival
The Jobele Festival
The Ogun Cleansing Rites
The Egungun Masquerade
questions.explanation: The counter-ritual is executed during the public Jobele festival, breaking Ajanaku's dark hold.

questions.text: What physical talisman is employed to sever Ajanaku's ritual power and heal Desola?
options: sacred cowrie gourd
consecrated red cloth wrapped around his neck accompanied by Desola's embrace
An iron broadsword quenched in palm wine
beaded leather wristband
questions.explanation: Iya Agba directs Odekunle to bind Ajanaku with the charmed red cloth as Desola embraces him to reverse the curse.

questions.text: What core message does the play deliver regarding tyrannical governance?
options: Absolute oppression can never be dismantled once established.
No matter how imposing a tyrant becomes, collective resolve and moral truth will bring about his downfall.
Communities must submit passively to authoritarian rulers.
Only external foreign armies can liberate an oppressed kingdom.
questions.explanation: The drama proves that hubristic despotism inevitably falls when a community unites with courage and ancestral truth.

questions.text: In Scene 1, what reason does Chief Serubawon give for hastening the coronation of Olaniyonu?
options: An invading army is at the city gates.
The throne must not remain vacant while the king lies hopelessly incapacitated.
The ancestors appeared to him in a direct daylight vision.
The farmers refused to harvest crops without an active monarch.
questions.explanation: Serubawon uses the king's persistent incapacitation to create a false emergency, pushing through the coronation.

questions.text: How does Odejimi characterize Serubawon's sudden coronation plans in Scene 1?
options: courageous rescue of the kingdom
treacherous, self-serving violation of sacred custom
profitable economic development
An honorable fulfillment of ancient treaties
questions.explanation: Odejimi denounces the rushed enthronement as an abomination that bypasses customary vetting and legitimacy.

questions.text: What argument does Iyale use when begging Odejimi to attend Ajanaku's coronation?
options: She wants him to demand higher taxes.
She fears the new ruler's wrath will destroy their household if he stays away.
She hopes Odekunle will be named royal general.
She believes Serubawon is truly acting in good faith.
questions.explanation: Iyale's plea is driven by self-preservation; she dreads the violent retribution an insecure tyrant visits on dissenters.

questions.text: How does Odejimi respond to his wife's fears of royal retaliation?
options: He relents and puts on his festive robe.
He declares that a man who compromises his conscience to save his neck is already dead.
He packs his household goods to escape into exile.
He appeals to Serubawon for private pardon.
questions.explanation: Odejimi asserts that moral compromise and fear are far worse than physical danger, standing on principle.

questions.text: What does Demoke advise Serubawon regarding Chief Odejimi's defiance?
options: To invite him for a peaceful banquet
To watch him carefully and crush his defiance before it infects the populace
To surrender the chieftaincy title to him
To apologize publicly to the hunter's guild
questions.explanation: Demoke displays a ruthless political streak, urging her husband to suppress Odejimi's principled dissent.

questions.text: When Iya Agba appears in the palace in Scene 3, how do the courtiers view her entrance?
options: With joy and musical celebration
With nervous shock, fear, and superstitious unease
With open amusement and laughter
With total indifference
questions.explanation: Her unannounced return from exile strikes fear into those who engineered her banishment.

questions.text: What metaphor does Iya Agba use to describe Ajanaku's inflated majesty?
options: deep well that never dries up
clay pot painted to look like bronze that will crack under fire
lion that hunts only at dusk
An iron mountain immovable by winds
questions.explanation: She compares his grandeur to a brittle clay pot masquerading as enduring bronze, destined to shatter.

questions.text: Why does Ajanaku refuse to execute Iya Agba on the spot when she defies him?
options: He respects her ancient wisdom.
He fears shedding royal blood directly in the courtyard and dismisses her as a harmless madwoman.
Serubawon begs him to spare her life.
The palace guards refuse to touch her.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku conceals his inner superstitious dread by feigning contempt, brushing her off as an inconsequential lunatic.

questions.text: Where do Odekunle and Desola arrange to meet away from parental scrutiny?
options: In the royal granary
Along the secluded bush path near the stream
Inside the shrine of Sango
At the central market stalls
questions.explanation: The young lovers meet along the quiet bush path to avoid the political animosity separating their families.

questions.text: What misgivings does Desola share with Odekunle during their meeting?
options: She wishes to marry a city merchant.
She feels a deep premonition of looming doom and fears her father's political ambitions.
She dislikes Odekunle's hunting duties.
She wants to leave her mother's household permanently.
questions.explanation: Desola expresses deep anxiety about her father's dangerous political games and senses impending misfortune.

questions.text: How is Odekunle incapacitated when King Ajanaku and his thugs ambush them?
options: He is shot with a poisoned arrow from behind.
He is blindsided, overpowered by superior numbers, and beaten unconscious.
He flees the scene in terror.
He is restrained by magical paralysis.
questions.explanation: Odekunle fights to shield Desola but is overwhelmed and battered senseless by Ajanaku's henchmen.

questions.text: What physical evidence does Odekunle present when he recounts the assault to his friends?
options: torn royal tunic
Bruised limbs, cuts, and Desola's dropped bead necklace
dropped royal flywhisk
broken hunter's bow
questions.explanation: Odekunle shows his wounds and Desola's broken ornaments, confirming the violent abduction.

questions.text: Who are Odekunle's hunter comrades who challenge his account of the skirmish?
options: Odegbami, Serubawon, and Ajasa
Yele, Lere, and Dele
Delani, Akinjobi, and Olaniyonu
Ogundele, Demoke, and Iyale
questions.explanation: Yele, Lere, and Dele are Odekunle's peers in the hunting guild who interrogate his account.

questions.text: What makes the hunters reluctant to march against the palace immediately?
options: They lack weapons and charms.
Ajanaku is the consecrated wearer of the crown, and regicide carries terrible ancestral consequences.
They support Ajanaku's land reforms.
They believe Desola eloped willingly.
questions.explanation: Direct armed rebellion against a consecrated monarch carries severe spiritual and societal penalties under custom.

questions.text: How does Demoke react when Desola is brought home unconscious and bleeding?
options: She blames Desola for wandering into the bush.
She wails in anguish, cursing the unknown predators who harmed her child.
She immediately accuses Iya Agba of witchcraft.
She demands that Serubawon celebrate the event.
questions.explanation: Demoke breaks down in grief, unaware that her own husband's political pawn committed the atrocity.

questions.text: What dark realization strikes Serubawon when he examines Desola's physical trauma?
options: She was bitten by a venomous viper.
Her injuries match the horrific symptoms of Ajanaku's Ijedodo virgin ritual.
She contracted a contagious epidemic.
She was beaten by rival market maidens.
questions.explanation: Serubawon recognizes the horrific physical signature of the very ritual he helped procure for Ajanaku.

questions.text: What does Serubawon do when he realizes Ajanaku violated his daughter?
options: He confronts Ajanaku with an army of palace guards.
He sinks into quiet terror, realizing he cannot openly condemn his creature without exposing himself.
He banishes Demoke from his home.
He resigns his chieftaincy post immediately.
questions.explanation: Serubawon is caught in a trap of his own making: exposing Ajanaku means exposing his own treason and complicity.

questions.text: Why does Iyale visit Iya Agba's forest dwelling?
options: To collect medicinal herbs for Odejimi's cough
To seek spiritual intervention and healing for the dying Desola
To purchase cowrie beads for a market trade
To warn her of royal assassins
questions.explanation: Knowing orthodox remedies are futile, Iyale turns to Iya Agba's esoteric knowledge to save Desola.

questions.text: What condition does Iya Agba set before agreeing to intervene on Desola's behalf?
options: payment of forty bags of cowries
Total truth, full disclosure of all past crimes, and genuine repentance from the conspirators
The immediate execution of Chief Serubawon
That Desola become a lifelong shrine devotee
questions.explanation: Iya Agba insists that spiritual healing requires unmasking every hidden truth and confessing past guilt.

questions.text: What does Iya Agba reveal about Adebisi's past in connection to Serubawon?
options: She was a royal princess who fled into the savanna.
She was the woman Serubawon secretly impregnated while married to Demoke, giving birth to Olaniyonu.
She was the herbalist who poisoned the legitimate king.
She was Iya Agba's younger sister.
questions.explanation: Adebisi was the mistress with whom Serubawon had Olaniyonu, making Ajanaku and Desola paternal half-siblings.

questions.text: What horrifying moral crime is committed through Ajanaku's assault on Desola?
options: Fratricide
Unwitting incest between paternal half-siblings
Matricide
Treason against foreign ambassadors
questions.explanation: Because Serubawon fathered both Ajanaku and Desola, the assault represents horrific incest, compounding the ritual atrocity.

questions.text: How does the revelation of incest affect Chief Serubawon's psychological state?
options: He dismisses it as a harmless coincidence.
It drives him into boundless horror, psychological collapse, and suicidal despair.
He blames his wife Demoke for keeping it secret.
He plots to poison Iya Agba immediately.
questions.explanation: The realization that his political machinations led his son to violate his daughter shatters Serubawon's psyche.

questions.text: What role does Delani play in the thematic critique of royal entitlement?
options: He shows that commoners can easily buy royal titles.
He embodies the oppressed subject whose rightful happiness is hijacked by monarchical greed.
He proves that hunters are naturally treacherous.
He acts as Ajanaku's chief tax collector.
questions.explanation: Delani's loss of Omoyeni demonstrates how ordinary citizens are stripped of dignity and happiness by predatory rulers.

questions.text: Why does Omoyeni resist Ajanaku's advances despite living in the royal palace?
options: She wishes to marry Chief Odejimi.
Her heart remains bound to Delani, and she views Ajanaku as a violent oppressor.
She wants to become the supreme kingmaker.
She refuses to wear traditional royal robes.
questions.explanation: Omoyeni views Ajanaku with contempt, keeping her love and loyalty anchored to Delani.

questions.text: How does King Ajanaku respond to Omoyeni's emotional coldness?
options: He releases her to return to her father's home.
He becomes increasingly insecure, volatile, and demanding, treating her as a possession.
He takes four additional wives to make her jealous.
He abdicates his throne to prove his devotion.
questions.explanation: Wounded vanity drives Ajanaku to become more tyrannical, treating her resistance as defiance against his absolute power.

questions.text: What does Omoyeni do when she realizes she is carrying Delani's child?
options: She attempts to terminate the pregnancy.
She flees to Iya Agba's sanctuary to protect the unborn life from the palace.
She claims Ajanaku is the father to secure wealth for the baby.
She leaves the kingdom with her father Ajasa.
questions.explanation: Omoyeni seeks safety with Iya Agba, safeguarding the child from palace plots.

questions.text: What major thematic commentary does the play offer on institutional sycophancy?
options: Sycophancy ensures lasting peace and community stability.
Sycophancy blinds despots to reality, accelerates administrative decay, and ends in ruin.
Praising a monarch constantly is a citizen's highest moral duty.
Courtiers should always support whatever ruler seizes power.
questions.explanation: The play shows that flattering despots breeds unchecked pride and shields them from the reality of their impending doom.

questions.text: How is dramatic irony sustained throughout Act Two regarding Desola's attacker?
options: The audience knows Odekunle attacked her, but the characters blame Ajanaku.
The audience knows Ajanaku is the perpetrator and Serubawon's son, while Serubawon only discovers it late.
The audience believes Desola fell from a palm tree.
The characters know the attacker, but the audience remains uninformed.
questions.explanation: The audience witnesses the dark connections early on, watching with dread as Serubawon slowly realizes his complicity.

questions.text: What does the Jobele festival celebrate in the traditional calendar of the town?
options: The coronation of the chief hunter
Communal renewal, harvest thanksgiving, and cultural solidarity
The commemoration of ancestral wars
The annual banishment of elders
questions.explanation: The Jobele festival is an annual gathering for harvest thanksgiving, communal cohesion, and renewal.

questions.text: Why does Ajanaku insist on appearing in full royal majesty at the Jobele festival?
options: He wants to announce reduced taxes for the peasants.
He intends to display his supposed invincibility and demand total submission from the populace.
He plans to surrender his crown to Odekunle.
He wishes to reconcile with Chief Odejimi.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku uses the public festival to showcase his absolute authority and demand uncritical worship.

questions.text: What role does the red cloth play in the counter-ritual devised by Iya Agba?
options: It serves as a royal coronation garment.
It is a consecrated talisman that binds and reverses the dark metaphysical power of the Ijedodo covenant.
It is a trade commodity brought from foreign merchants.
It signals the arrival of the hunters' guild.
questions.explanation: The red cloth functions as a targeted spiritual antidote that neutralizes the demonic covenant of the virgin sacrifice.

questions.text: Why must Desola physically embrace Ajanaku to complete the counter-ritual?
options: To beg for his royal mercy
To reconnect the stolen life essence back to its rightful owner and break the curse
To demonstrate forgiveness in front of the townspeople
To distract the palace guards while the hunters draw their weapons
questions.explanation: The embrace reclaims the vital essence stolen during the ritual assault, breaking the spell and healing the victim.

questions.text: What happens to King Ajanaku the moment the counter-ritual is executed at the festival?
options: He transforms into an actual elephant and flees into the savanna.
His artificial metaphysical invulnerability shatters, and he collapses in agonizing, helpless ruin.
He draws his sword and executes Chief Odejimi.
He disappears into thin air.
questions.explanation: His mystical protection shatters, and the stolen vitality drains away, leaving him broken and helpless.

questions.text: How do the townspeople react when they see Ajanaku fall in the festival square?
options: They wail and mourn his passing.
They break into jubilant celebrations of liberation, recognizing that the tyrant's reign is broken.
They attack Chief Odejimi in anger.
They flee the town in fear of divine wrath.
questions.explanation: The populace celebrates with relief, rejoicing that the reign of terror has been broken.

questions.text: What happens to the dying Desola once the counter-ritual is completed?
options: She dies immediately from exhaustion.
Her vital energy is restored, and she regains her physical strength and life.
She loses her eyesight permanently.
She falls into an eternal coma.
questions.explanation: Reclaiming her stolen spiritual essence breaks the wasting affliction, restoring Desola to vibrant health.

questions.text: What lesson does Demoke learn from the tragedy that struck her household?
options: That palace wealth is the only thing worth pursuing
That treachery and past conspiracies inevitably rebound to consume one's own children
That she should have supported Ajanaku more aggressively
That hunters are more dangerous than monarchs
questions.explanation: Demoke realizes that framing Iya Agba and helping Serubawon rise through deceit sowed seeds of ruin for her own family.

questions.text: What happens to Oba Akinjobi after the fall of Ajanaku?
options: He dies and is buried in the forest.
His illness lifts with the breaking of the dark spells, restoring legitimate ancestral order.
He abdicates and moves to another town.
He names Odekunle as the new monarch.
questions.explanation: The spiritual purification of the realm breaks the demonic affliction holding the legitimate king, restoring order.

questions.text: How does the play resolve the romantic conflict between Delani and Omoyeni?
options: Delani rejects her because she lived in the palace.
Their love is validated, and they are reunited along with their child.
Omoyeni is exiled with the baby.
Delani leaves the kingdom to join a foreign army.
questions.explanation: Justice prevails: Delani and Omoyeni are reunited in freedom to raise their child together without palace terror.

questions.text: What future awaits Odekunle and Desola at the conclusion of the play?
options: They separate due to the family scandals.
Their love endures the trial, paving the way for their marriage and healing between the houses.
Odekunle leaves the hunters' guild to live as a hermit.
Desola becomes a priestess of the earth shrine.
questions.explanation: With Desola healed and the dark curse lifted, the young lovers look forward to a restored future.

questions.text: Which dramatic movement best captures the ideological tone of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Absurdist drama
Social realist and satirical indigenous African drama
Classical Elizabethan romantic farce
Pure existentialist melodrama
questions.explanation: The play blends African oral performance traditions with social realism to satirize political corruption and tyranny.

questions.text: How does Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan utilize oral performance devices in the text?
options: By writing exclusively in rhymed English iambic pentameter
By incorporating proverbs, dirges, festive chants, incantations, and praise poetry (Oriki)
By eliminating all musical instrumentation from the stage
By using European chorus conventions exclusively
questions.explanation: The play draws on total African theater, integrating proverbs, chanting, drums, and lyrical oral traditions.

questions.text: What do the proverbs spoken by Chief Odejimi reflect about his character?
options: His desire to confuse the townspeople
His deep grounding in ancestral philosophy, wisdom, and unyielding moral truth
His cowardice when speaking to rulers
His ambition to become the new chief priest
questions.explanation: Odejimi's mastery of proverbs reflects his moral depth and grounding in ancestral wisdom and custom.

questions.text: What is the function of the crowd and townspeople in the festival scene?
options: They act as decorative stage extras without dialogue.
They represent the civic body, providing a gauge of public sentiment from fear to triumphant defiance.
They represent foreign mercenaries supporting Ajanaku.
They serve as comedic relief.
questions.explanation: The crowd reflects the communal consciousness, illustrating the journey from cowed submission to active resistance.

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of gender in traditional power structures?
options: Women are shown as entirely helpless victims who play no part in civic life.
Women like Iya Agba and Iyale are central to preserving memory, moral resistance, and spiritual restoration.
Women are portrayed as the primary architects of military violence.
Women are excluded from all scenes involving traditional customs.
questions.explanation: The playwright highlights the vital agency of women, positioning them as keepers of truth and catalysts of redemption.

questions.text: What warning does the play provide concerning leaders who divorce power from responsibility?
options: Such leaders achieve enduring international respect.
Power exercised without justice becomes predatory and sows the seeds of its own destruction.
Citizens will naturally revere ruthless strength above ethical leadership.
Spiritual deities have no concern with human justice.
questions.explanation: The drama shows that authority detached from justice becomes monstrous and inevitably collapses under its own abuses.

questions.text: What does the sacred crown (Ade) symbolize when worn by an illegitimate ruler like Ajanaku?
options: The absolute forgiveness of all crimes
desecrated symbol of authority that torments the usurper and brings judgment upon the land
guarantee of military victory
commercial asset that can be traded for weapons
questions.explanation: On a usurper's brow, the crown is a spiritual burden that mocks his illegitimacy and demands ancestral reckoning.

questions.text: What is the dramatic effect of staging the climax during a festive public celebration like Jobele?
options: It allows the actors to perform comedic dances.
It maximizes theatrical impact by unmasking the tyrant's shame before the entire assembled community.
It saves money on costume changes.
It keeps the action hidden from the common people.
questions.explanation: Staging the denouement during a civic festival ensures the tyrant's public unmasking and collective liberation.

questions.text: How does the language of Ajanaku evolve as his power becomes more unhinged?
options: It becomes increasingly polite and philosophical.
It shifts from political persuasion to megalomaniacal, boastful, and dismissive threats.
He ceases speaking and communicates only through drumbeats.
He speaks entirely in foreign loanwords.
questions.explanation: His speech shifts into grand, boastful declarations of invincibility, reflecting his slide into tyrannical delusion.

questions.text: What does Serubawon's name literally suggest in Yoruba onomastics?
options: Bringer of rainfall
One who instills fear or terror in others
The peaceful farmer
The hunter of antelopes
questions.explanation: 'Serubawon' translates to 'frighten them' or 'instill terror in them,' signaling his intimidating political nature.

questions.text: What does the name 'Ajanaku' mean in Yoruba culture and lore?
options: The clever hare
The mighty Elephant
The swift leopard
The resilient weaver bird
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is the traditional poetic name for the elephant, embodying colossal, untamed physical power.

questions.text: What role does the off-stage presence of the incapacitated Oba Akinjobi play in the plot?
options: He serves as an irrelevant historical detail.
He remains a moral reference point, reminding the audience of legitimate order subverted by conspiracy.
He orchestrates the assassination of Serubawon from his bed.
He represents foreign colonial influence.
questions.explanation: The bedridden king symbolizes interrupted legitimacy, keeping the necessity of restoration before the audience.

questions.text: How does the play portray the vulnerability of youth under tyrannical regimes?
options: Youth are completely insulated from political developments.
Young people like Desola, Odekunle, and Omoyeni are assaulted, commodified, and sacrificed to elite ambition.
Youth are the primary instigators of palace coups.
Young characters easily overpower corrupt elders from the opening scene.
questions.explanation: The youth bear the brunt of autocratic depravity, suffering physical assault, exploitation, and lost innocence.

questions.text: What is the function of drum language in the performance of the play?
options: To entertain the actors during stage transitions
To communicate warnings, herald royal arrivals, punctuate emotional shifts, and invoke ancestral power
To replace spoken dialogue completely
To mimic modern European military parades
questions.explanation: Talking drums serve a rich dramatic function, commenting on the action, signaling danger, and evoking spiritual weight.

questions.text: Why is Chief Odejimi's refusal to attend the coronation an act of extraordinary courage?
options: Because Ajanaku had already pardoned him
Because defying an absolute ruler invites execution, confiscation of goods, and destruction of his family
Because his wife commanded him to remain indoors
Because he had lost his chieftaincy regalia
questions.explanation: Publicly boycotting a despot's enthronement constitutes treason, risking immediate execution and ruin.

questions.text: How does the play handle the concept of 'Ewo' (taboo or spiritual prohibition)?
options: As a set of harmless superstitions to be discarded by modern leaders
As immutable moral and cosmic boundaries that, when broken by greed, trigger catastrophic retribution
As rules meant only for slaves and commoners
As guidelines that kings can alter at will
questions.explanation: Taboos (Ewo) represent cosmic laws; violating them through incest and ritual murder triggers cosmic retribution.

questions.text: What contrast is established between the compound of Chief Odejimi and the Royal Palace?
options: Odejimi's compound is a place of poverty and despair, while the palace is peaceful.
Odejimi's home represents integrity, truth, and familial harmony, while the palace is a pit of deceit, fear, and paranoia.
Both spaces are identical in moral atmosphere.
The palace is empty, while Odejimi's house is overflowing with royal guards.
questions.explanation: The modest home of Odejimi radiates moral clarity, contrasting sharply with the opulent paranoia of the palace.

questions.text: What does the playwright suggest about the role of ordinary citizens in ending oppression?
options: Citizens should wait for the gods to strike down oppressors without human effort.
Liberation requires moral courage, speaking unvarnished truth, and collective civic action.
Citizens should leave their homelands whenever misrule occurs.
Citizens should appease tyrants with richer gifts.
questions.explanation: The play emphasizes human agency: divine and cosmic balance is restored when people stand together against injustice.

questions.text: How does Iya Agba's cottage on the outskirts of the town function dramatically?
options: As a prison where she is guarded day and night
As an alternative sanctuary of historical truth, spiritual healing, and moral clarity away from court corruption
As a marketplace stall for selling charms to foreign hunters
As an armory for weapons of war
questions.explanation: Her cottage acts as a sanctuary of truth and restorative power away from the compromised palace.

questions.text: What does the phrase 'Once Upon an Elephant' itself evoke in the reader's imagination?
options: factual history textbook on colonial forestry
fable or parable opening that warns of the rise and fall of monstrous power
light comedy for kindergarten storytelling
An instruction manual on big-game hunting
questions.explanation: The title uses folktale framing to signal an allegorical fable on the intoxicating nature and fall of tyrannical power.

questions.text: What is the ultimate cathartic impact of the play's conclusion?
options: It leaves the audience in hopeless existential despair.
It delivers moral and spiritual relief as justice is restored, the tyrant falls, and the wounded are healed.
It ends in unresolved civil war and total destruction.
It celebrates the success of political deceit.
questions.explanation: The climax provides powerful catharsis: the tyrant's defeat restores order, heals the innocent, and validates moral courage.

questions.text: What internal conflict torments Chief Serubawon after Ajanaku is successfully installed on the throne?
options: He regrets not crowning himself directly.
He realizes that the puppet king he created has grown into an uncontrollable, menacing monster who ignores his counsel.
He worries that the British colonial officers will depose him.
He fears that Oba Akinjobi has recovered his physical strength.
questions.explanation: Serubawon realizes too late that his handpicked puppet has transformed into an uncontrollable tyrant.

questions.text: Why does Ajanaku feel an obsessive need to attain physical immortality through the Ijedodo ritual?
options: He wants to preserve his youth for his wives.
Deep insecurity and gnawing terror that his fraudulent usurpation will be overturned by mortality and vengeance.
The oracle of Ifa commanded him to rule forever.
He wants to lead military conquests for a century.
questions.explanation: Illegitimate rulers live in constant paranoia; Ajanaku seeks magical immortality to escape the reckoning he knows he deserves.

questions.text: How does Odekunle's character demonstrate the transition from impetuous youth to mature warrior?
options: By abandoning hunting to become a palace tax collector.
By channeling his rage into disciplined alignment with ancestral guidance and courageous action during the counter-ritual.
By running away to an adjacent town when Desola is abducted.
By challenging his father Chief Odejimi to a wrestling duel.
questions.explanation: Odekunle matures from a hotheaded youth into a disciplined warrior who follows ancestral direction to liberate his people.

questions.text: What makes Iyale's maternal role crucial in breaking the cycle of catastrophe?
options: She organizes a violent protest of women against the king's palace.
She bridges the divide by putting aside political grudges to seek Iya Agba's healing help for Desola.
She shoots King Ajanaku with an enchanted arrow.
She convinces Chief Odejimi to flee into self-imposed exile.
questions.explanation: Iyale rises above factional hostility, bringing the dying daughter of her husband's enemy to Iya Agba for healing.

questions.text: How does Demoke's past complicity in framing Iya Agba mirror the larger political decay of the realm?
options: It shows that women had complete legal control over royal lands.
It reveals how personal malice and deceit by palace insiders subverted righteous leadership long before Ajanaku's reign.
It proves that the royal house was impoverished.
It demonstrates that traditional justice was always corrupt.
questions.explanation: Demoke's historical lie shows that Ajanaku's tyranny did not emerge from a vacuum; it grew from years of moral decay among palace elites.

questions.text: What psychological motive drives Ajanaku's forced marriage to Omoyeni?
options: Genuine romantic devotion and emotional tenderness
desire to exert absolute dominance over all things, treating human beings and love as trophies of royal conquest.
treaty obligation made with Chief Ajasa
The spiritual instructions of the Olubori rites
questions.explanation: For Ajanaku, claiming Omoyeni is an exercise in domination: an autocrat takes what he wants simply to demonstrate that none can refuse him.

questions.text: Why does Chief Ajasa give his daughter Omoyeni to King Ajanaku despite her prior betrothal to Delani?
options: He hated Delani's family lineage.
Spineless opportunism and fear of monarchical power, prioritizing proximity to royalty over honor and parental duty.
Ajanaku gave him half of the kingdom's gold.
Omoyeni begged him to allow her into the palace.
questions.explanation: Ajasa represents the spineless elder who trades his own daughter's happiness to appease power and gain favor.

questions.text: What distinguishes Chief Odejimi's brand of courage from mere recklessness?
options: He fights only when he has twenty armed hunters beside him.
His courage is anchored on moral principle, respect for ancestral legitimacy, and refusal to normalize falsehood.
He waits until Ajanaku is asleep before speaking against him.
He consults foreign warriors to protect his farm.
questions.explanation: True courage is rooted in moral clarity; Odejimi stands firm not out of bravado, but out of devotion to truth and justice.

questions.text: How does Iya Agba embody the archetype of the 'Wise Old Woman' in African folklore?
options: She lives in a golden palace and dictates military campaigns.
She retains ancestral memory, understands herbal and metaphysical mysteries, and diagnoses moral sickness.
She casts malevolent curses on any traveler who walks near her home.
She refuses to speak to anyone who does not bring bags of salt.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba preserves the community's moral memory, dispenses spiritual healing, and exposes the roots of hidden guilt.

questions.text: What does Delani's steadfast devotion to Omoyeni demonstrate amidst prevailing court corruption?
options: That romantic love is foolish during political struggles
That genuine love, fidelity, and moral constancy endure even when assaulted by tyrannical power.
That common hunters should never seek wives outside their clan
That he was secretly conspiring with the royal guards
questions.explanation: Delani's enduring love shines against palace treachery, proving that virtue and affection outlast tyrannical overreach.

questions.text: How does Desola's friendship with Yosola contrast with the relationships among the palace elders?
options: It is built on commercial transactions and bribes.
It is marked by innocence, mutual care, and honesty, contrasting with the suspicion and deceit among the elders.
Yosola is secretly plotting to displace Desola.
They compete fiercely for the king's attention.
questions.explanation: The girls' innocent friendship provides a refreshing contrast to the deceit, suspicion, and greed of the court elites.

questions.text: What does Serubawon's suicide signify within the ethical framework of Yoruba tragic drama?
options: cowardly escape that clears his name entirely
The ultimate, unavoidable consequence of cosmic shame, self-judgment, and traditional reckoning for unforgivable abominations.
religious requirement to ensure his son remains on the throne
An accident resulting from a poisoned hunting knife
questions.explanation: In classical Yoruba tradition, suicide is the final recourse for a leader whose crimes are too monstrous for society to absorb.

questions.text: Why is King Ajanaku blind to the impending danger at the Jobele festival?
options: His eyes were afflicted with a physical sickness.
His arrogance and belief that the completed Ijedodo ritual made him a god blinded him to mortal and divine reality.
Serubawon assured him that no hunters would be present.
The townspeople gave him poisoned palm wine.
questions.explanation: Hubris produces fatal blindness: convinced of his immortality, Ajanaku walks into his own destruction.

questions.text: How does the Hunters' Guild demonstrate the concept of communal solidarity during the crisis?
options: They abandon the village to hunt in distant provinces.
They close ranks, overcome early divisions, and coordinate with ancestral wisdom to liberate the realm.
They elect Odekunle as their absolute ruler.
They burn down the palace without consulting the elders.
questions.explanation: The hunters unite and act in concert with ancestral wisdom to dismantle the oppressive regime.

questions.text: What does the character of Adebisi, though absent from the physical stage, represent in the backstory?
options: foreign queen who invaded the territory
The hidden, buried moral compromises of the past whose unacknowledged fruit (Ajanaku) returns to terrorize the present.
The royal priestess who crowned King Akinjobi
The market queen who built the town square
questions.explanation: Adebisi represents the buried transgressions of the past whose hidden consequences resurface to threaten the entire community.

questions.text: How does Chief Odejimi treat his son Odekunle after the assault on Desola?
options: He disowns him for losing a fight.
He listens with parental empathy, assesses the political danger, and channels his grief toward strategic, moral action.
He commands him to marry another maiden immediately.
He hands him over to Serubawon's guards.
questions.explanation: Odejimi listens with fatherly wisdom, transforming his son's raw pain into focused, principled action.

questions.text: Why does Omoyeni refuse to abort the pregnancy despite the dangerous suspicions of the palace?
options: She wants to blackmail King Ajanaku for land.
She cherishes the life fathered by her true lover Delani and refuses to sacrifice innocent blood to court terror.
The palace physicians forbade any medicine.
Her father Ajasa commanded her to keep the child.
questions.explanation: Omoyeni views the unborn baby as a sacred pledge of her love for Delani, refusing to destroy it.

questions.text: What is the psychological impact of the Ijedodo ritual on the town's collective morale?
options: It unites the people in worship of the new king.
It casts a suffocating shroud of terror, paranoia, and moral outrage over families with young daughters.
It encourages the farmers to clear more land.
It attracts foreign merchants to the community market.
questions.explanation: The disappearance and wasting deaths of young maidens terrorize families and destroy communal security.

questions.text: How does Ajanaku respond when his advisors express caution regarding public anger?
options: He listens and reduces the tax burden.
He ridicules their cowardice, boasts of his terrifying power, and demands harsher crackdowns on dissenters.
He steps down from the throne for seven days.
He seeks the counsel of Chief Odejimi.
questions.explanation: The despot dismisses prudent counsel as weakness, responding to public grumbling with harsher repression.

questions.text: What does the restoration of Desola's health signify for the kingdom's future?
options: That the royal lineage has ended permanently
That the wounded, innocent generation can heal and flourish once the roots of evil and oppression are uprooted.
That she must marry a new foreign prince
That the hunters must surrender their weapons
questions.explanation: Desola's recovery proves that the traumas inflicted by tyranny can be healed once corruption is purged.

questions.text: What theatrical device opens Scene 1 to establish the rising political crisis?
options: cheerful harvest dance by young maidens
Solemn, urgent dialogue between conspirators plotting to fill the throne amidst ominous drum beats
comedic argument between market women
An elaborate military march across the stage
questions.explanation: Scene 1 begins with tense, conspiratorial dialogue set against ominous drumming, establishing the political crisis.

questions.text: How does the playwright use spatial settings (palace vs. forest vs. cottage) to reinforce thematic tensions?
options: The settings are completely interchangeable with no symbolic meaning.
The palace represents corrupt power, the forest represents untamed trial, and Iya Agba's cottage represents restorative truth.
All scenes take place exclusively inside Serubawon's compound.
The settings represent different modern urban office spaces.
questions.explanation: The settings reflect the play's themes: the palace is a center of corruption, the forest tests courage, and the cottage shelters wisdom.

questions.text: What dramatic purpose is served by placing Desola's ambush in a secluded bush path rather than the palace?
options: It saves on stage lighting costs.
It highlights the vulnerability of ordinary life outside fortified compounds and the predatory reach of the tyrant.
It allows Odekunle to use a bow and arrow.
It shows that Desola was trying to leave the kingdom.
questions.explanation: Setting the ambush on the pathway dramatizes how the tyrant's violence reaches into everyday spaces.

questions.text: How does the dialogue in the Hunters' Guild meeting in Scene 8 generate dramatic tension?
options: Through silent pantomime without words
Through fiery debate between passionate youth demanding immediate rebellion and cautious elders wary of sacrilege
By having the hunters recite ancient praise songs for King Ajanaku
By having the hunters vote on meat prices
questions.explanation: Tension crackles between impatient young hunters demanding action and cautious elders navigating the taboo of regicide.

questions.text: What is the function of the soliloquy delivered by Serubawon when he is alone in his chamber?
options: To explain his financial investments in cowries
To expose his inner torment, gnawing guilt, and realization that his own ambition has destroyed his family
To practice his praise poetry for the upcoming festival
To mock Chief Odejimi's agricultural harvest
questions.explanation: His soliloquy lays bare his unraveling psyche and agony as he realizes his daughter has fallen victim to his own scheme.

questions.text: How does the pacing of the play accelerate between Scene 10 and Scene 14?
options: The scenes become longer with leisurely philosophical discussions.
The scenes become shorter, more urgent, and rapidly alternate between the cottage, the palace, and the festival grounds.
The playwright eliminates all characters except Ajanaku.
The dialogue shifts into prose chronicles read by a narrator.
questions.explanation: Rapid scene shifts between parallel locations build dramatic tension as the confrontation approaches.

questions.text: What auditory element is used to signal the beginning of the Jobele festival in Scene 13?
options: Total stage silence for five minutes
Vibrant, complex festival drumming combining praise beats with dissonant ancestral undertones
European trumpet flourishes
The sound of modern gunfire
questions.explanation: Layered festival drumming sets the stage, mixing public celebration with tense undertones of impending confrontation.

questions.text: How is King Ajanaku's costume at the festival designed to reflect his psychological state?
options: He wears ragged clothing to display false humility.
He is dressed in flamboyant, heavy royal regalia, beaded crown, and ornaments that emphasize his hubris and visual bulk.
He wears simple hunter's leather garments.
He appears in white priestly vestments without beads.
questions.explanation: His heavy, ostentatious costume visually mirrors his pride and elephantine vanity.

questions.text: What visual contrast is created when the frail, recovering Desola approaches the imposing King Ajanaku?
options: contrast between two equally matched warriors
stark visual contrast between innocent vulnerability and towering, monstrous tyranny
comedic encounter between two performers
formal diplomatic exchange between monarchs
questions.explanation: The contrast between the frail girl and the hulking despot visually distills the play's moral conflict.

questions.text: What is the dramatic effect of having Odekunle wrap the charmed red cloth around Ajanaku from behind?
options: It allows Ajanaku to easily push him away.
It creates a heart-stopping moment of suspense where mortal danger and ancestral justice hang in the balance.
It produces comedic laughter among the crowd.
It stops all music and dancing instantly.
questions.explanation: The sudden binding creates suspense: one misstep by Odekunle could unleash the despot's wrath.

questions.text: How do the stage directions describe Ajanaku's physical collapse during the counter-ritual?
options: He bows gracefully and exits the stage.
He staggers, groans in sudden weakness, grasps his throat, and crashes heavily to the earth like a felled tree.
He sits calmly on his throne and closes his eyes.
He leaps into the air and runs off-stage.
questions.explanation: Stage directions portray a dramatic fall: he staggers, clutches his throat, and hits the ground like a collapsing elephant.

questions.text: What role does lighting play during the scenes set inside Iya Agba's cottage?
options: Blinding neon lights that highlight every modern corner
Warm, flickering earthen light that suggests ancient mysteries, safety, and ancestral presence
Pitch-black darkness where actors cannot be seen
Strobe lights indicating a thunderstorm
questions.explanation: Warm, earthen lighting creates an atmosphere of timeless sanctuary and spiritual grounding.

questions.text: How does the playwright maintain thematic unity throughout fourteen scenes?
options: By having every scene end with the exact same sentence
By anchoring every plot thread to the central allegory of unbridled power and the inevitable reckoning of the usurper
By featuring only two actors who play multiple roles
By confining the entire plot to a single calendar day
questions.explanation: Every subplot—the succession, the assault, the young lovers—ties back to the consequences of tyrannical overreach.

questions.text: What is the function of dramatic pauses and silences during Iya Agba's interrogations of the conspirators?
options: The actors forgot their written dialogue.
To allow truth to weigh heavily in the space, compelling the guilty to confront their inner shame.
To give the musicians time to tune their instruments
To invite audience members to shout answers
questions.explanation: Deliberate silences create moral tension, forcing characters to face the weight of their buried deeds.

questions.text: How does the final tableau (the concluding visual arrangement of actors on stage) communicate restoration?
options: The stage is left completely empty with corpses scattered around.
The fallen tyrant lies isolated while the restored lovers, elders, and community gather together in unity and light.
Chief Serubawon stands triumphant above the throne.
King Ajanaku is carried off on the shoulders of his guards.
questions.explanation: The closing stage picture isolates the fallen tyrant while surrounding the reunited community in light.

questions.text: What is the linguistic style of the dialogue between Chief Odejimi and Chief Serubawon?
options: Broken Pidgin English with slapstick jokes
Elevated, proverb-rich, and metaphorically dense traditional rhetoric characteristic of Yoruba elder statesmanship
Academic legalistic English resembling modern court proceedings
Monosyllabic, rapid insults without cultural references
questions.explanation: Their exchanges feature dignified, proverb-laden dialogue fitting senior custodians of custom.

questions.text: How does the playwright handle the depiction of physical violence on stage?
options: With gratuitous, graphic gore that distracts from the political theme
Through disciplined, stylized dramatic action that emphasizes moral and psychological impact over mere spectacle
By cutting away to recorded modern film clips
By having all violence occur off-stage without any visual representation
questions.explanation: Action is staged with dramatic discipline, focusing on moral and psychological consequences rather than shock value.

questions.text: What purpose does the recurring motif of the royal bead necklace serve on stage?
options: It is a prop used strictly for commercial trade.
It acts as a physical emblem of royal legitimacy, which becomes tainted when associated with violence and theft.
It is used by Odekunle to bind game animals in the forest.
It is given to foreign messengers as a passport.
questions.explanation: Beads symbolize consecrated authority; when worn by a violent usurper, they serve as a visible badge of corruption.

questions.text: How does the Chorus of Market Women in Scene 6 contribute to the play's socio-economic critique?
options: They sing praises of the king's wonderful tax policies.
They voice the biting reality of food scarcity, exorbitant levies, and the daily suffering of commoners under the new regime.
They announce that they are moving their stalls to the capital city.
They refuse to sell food to anyone except palace guards.
questions.explanation: The market women voice the economic toll of misrule, highlighting sky-high food prices and extortionate levies.

questions.text: What makes the play's resolution characteristic of traditional African communal reconciliation rather than nihilistic tragedy?
options: Every single character in the kingdom is executed by the gods.
The community does not perish in despair; rather, the evil is excised, life is affirmed, and the moral order is renewed.
The tyrant wakes up and laughs, revealing it was all a dream.
The kingdom is annexed by an aggressive foreign empire.
questions.explanation: Rather than collapsing into despair, the drama affirms life, purging the rot and renewing the community.

questions.text: Complete the proverb used by Iya Agba: 'The bird that dances on the pathway...'
options: ...has built its nest in the sky.
...has its drummer beating the rhythms in the nearby bush.
...will be caught by the hunter's dog before evening.
...knows the secrets of the cloud.
questions.explanation: The proverb signifies that a boastful puppet king is merely dancing to hidden rhythms drummed by conspirators.

questions.text: What does the proverb 'The stream that forgets its source will surely dry up' warn against in the play?
options: Digging irrigation wells near the farm
leader who turns his back on ancestral heritage, moral foundations, and traditional limits will meet ruin.
Hunters who drink river water during night expeditions
Market women who hike the price of fresh fish
questions.explanation: It warns that rulers who abandon ancestral principles and moral accountability dry up their own mandate.

questions.text: When Chief Odejimi says, 'You cannot cover the smoke of a burning roof with a hand basket,' what does he mean?
options: The palace needs better building materials.
Monstrous crimes, treason, and usurpation cannot be concealed by superficial ceremonies and lies.
Hunters must bring water buckets to every meeting.
Serubawon should construct a brick ceiling.
questions.explanation: The proverb emphasizes that colossal crimes cannot be whitewashed by superficial titles and lies.

questions.text: Who said the following lines: 'Let those who think they are elephants remember that the forest has pits deeper than their bulk'?
options: Chief Serubawon to Demoke
Iya Agba to the palace courtiers
Ajanaku to Chief Ajasa
Yosola to Desola
questions.explanation: Iya Agba delivers this warning, reminding courtiers that pride will not save a tyrant from the pit.

questions.text: What is the meaning of the traditional praise chant applied ironically to Ajanaku: 'O pa ma l'eku, o pa ma l'agbo'?
options: He who farms yams without clearing the grass
He who slays without sparing, whose steps shake the earth
The generous provider of fish and palm oil
The gentle father of all royal orphans
questions.explanation: The praise chant highlights frightening, destructive power—a title of terror turned back upon the oppressor.

questions.text: What does the proverb 'When the head is severed, what becomes of the cap?' imply about Serubawon's relationship to Ajanaku?
options: The weavers must craft new crowns for the prince.
When the mastermind of conspiracy falls, all his artificial titles and creations will collapse with him.
Hunters should never hunt without leather hats.
The king's crown is too heavy for a young man.
questions.explanation: It emphasizes that artificial creations collapse when their scheming architect is brought down.

questions.text: When Ajanaku boasts, 'I am the boulder that breaks the pestle that dares to pound it,' which figure of speech is he using?
options: Hyperbolic metaphor reflecting his megalomania
Understatement describing his modesty
Euphemism regarding his royal diet
Oxymoron showing his deep religious faith
questions.explanation: Comparing himself to an unbreakable boulder is a bombastic metaphor illustrating his delusions of grandeur.

questions.text: What rhetorical purpose does Iya Agba's deployment of riddles serve when speaking to Chief Serubawon?
options: She wants to play entertaining games with him.
She uses riddles to disarm his political defenses, expose his hidden crimes, and force him to judge himself.
She has lost the ability to speak clearly.
She wants him to buy her garden produce.
questions.explanation: Riddles allow her to dismantle his pretenses and guide him to recognize his guilt.

questions.text: Who exclaims, 'The crown on a thief's head does not turn him into an Oba; it only makes the crown an accessory to robbery'?
options: Demoke
Chief Odejimi
Ajasa
Ajanaku
questions.explanation: Odejimi cuts through royal pretensions, pointing out that regalia cannot legitimize a usurper.

questions.text: What traditional concept is embedded in the saying: 'Blood spilled in secret cries out from the pebbles'?
options: The river contains iron mineral wealth.
The moral and cosmic belief that hidden crimes and ritual murders cannot remain concealed forever.
Hunters must wash their feet after entering the town.
Ancestors require wine offerings every Friday.
questions.explanation: This Yoruba metaphysical concept asserts that murder leaves an indelible mark that demands cosmic reckoning.

questions.text: How does Chief Serubawon address Ajanaku when trying to caution him in Scene 9?
options: With harsh curses and physical threats
With a mixture of paternal familiarity, desperate advice, and growing fear of the monster he created
With cold indifference as if to a stranger
With foreign diplomatic salutations
questions.explanation: Serubawon vacillates between paternal advice and creeping dread as he realizes he has lost control.

questions.text: What is Ajanaku's dismissive retort when Serubawon warns him that the town elders are grumbling?
options: 'I will invite them to share my royal meal.'
'Let them grumble until their throats dry out! Can the barking of dogs ever stop the journey of an elephant?'
'I will pack my robes and return to farming.'
'Tell them Chief Odejimi will address their concerns.'
questions.explanation: He scoffs at the elders' discontent, comparing public dissent to dogs barking uselessly at an elephant.

questions.text: What does the phrase 'Olubori' literally imply in the context of royal coronation rites?
options: The master of the fishing nets
The conqueror of destinies / The ruler whose head triumphs over all heads
The builder of city walls
The keeper of the king's horses
questions.explanation: 'Olubori' evokes headship, destiny, and supremacy over all other heads in the realm.

questions.text: When Desola regains consciousness and whispers, 'Mother, the beast had the eyes of a king,' what literary device is used?
options: Hyperbole
Paradoxical revelation / Dramatic unmasking
Comic irony
Onomatopoeia
questions.explanation: Her words cut to the heart of the play's horror: the monster terrorizing the bush path sits on the throne.

questions.text: What does Iyale mean when she tells Demoke: 'We do not look at a child's face to determine whose house has caught fire'?
options: Children should be sent to fetch water from the stream.
When disaster strikes innocent youth, all factional enmities must be forgotten to save lives.
Every compound must build higher fences.
Demoke should leave her daughter in the palace.
questions.explanation: Iyale asserts that helping an innocent child in mortal danger supersedes adult quarrels.

questions.text: Which proverb summarizes the ultimate fate of Chief Serubawon?
options: 'The patient dog eats the fattest bone.'
'He who digs a pit of deceit for another will surely tumble into its bottom.'
'A rolling stone gathers no moss.'
'The early bird catches the morning worm.'
questions.explanation: Serubawon's downfall is a textbook example of falling into the very pit of deceit he dug for others.

questions.text: What rhetorical tone characterizes Iya Agba's chants during the preparation of the red cloth counter-ritual?
options: Timid and apologetic
Authoritative, incisive, solemn, and charged with metaphysical certainty
Frantic and confused
Mournful and defeated
questions.explanation: She speaks with authoritative certainty, channeling ancestral power to dismantle the curse.

questions.text: When Odekunle states, 'My bow was not carved to shoot shadows, but tonight the shadow wears a crown,' what does he mean?
options: He wants to practice archery at midnight.
He recognizes that his hunt is no longer for bush game, but for an oppressive, illegitimate ruler.
He is complaining about poor stage lighting.
He believes King Ajanaku is a phantom spirit.
questions.explanation: He realizes that his hunting skills must be directed toward confronting the tyrant on the throne.

questions.text: What is the thematic significance of the final choral chant: 'The earth has reclaimed its own'?
options: The farmers are ready to plant corn.
Cosmic and ecological balance has been restored by purging the unnatural usurper from the throne.
The townspeople must relocate to another province.
All hunters must bury their iron spears.
questions.explanation: The closing chant celebrates the land's spiritual cleansing and the return of moral and ecological balance.

questions.text: How does Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan's use of language elevate the drama beyond everyday prose?
options: By translating modern British slang into archaic forms
By weaving philosophical proverbs, rhythmic chants, and rich cultural imagery into the core dramatic action
By avoiding complex vocabulary completely
By using only Latin phrases for legal matters
questions.explanation: The dramatist enriches the play with proverbs, chants, and cultural metaphors, elevating it into poetic theater.

questions.text: In a WAEC-standard examination essay, what is the most accurate classification of Ajanaku's role?
options: Comic foil
Tragic antagonist and tyrannical usurper
Benevolent mentor
Neutral observer
questions.explanation: Ajanaku functions as the tragic antagonist whose hubris and violent usurpation drive the central conflict.

questions.text: Which character serves as the primary protagonist and moral compass among the community elders?
options: Chief Serubawon
Chief Odejimi
Chief Ajasa
Ajanaku
questions.explanation: Chief Odejimi stands as the moral compass of the community, modeling unyielding integrity.

questions.text: What major dramatic technique is exemplified when the audience knows Ajanaku assaulted Desola while her father Serubawon does not?
options: Deus ex machina
Dramatic irony
Pathetic fallacy
Stream of consciousness
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience understands crucial truths that remain hidden from characters on stage.

questions.text: How does the playwright depict the relationship between political power and traditional spirituality?
options: Spirituality is completely separate from political governance.
Political authority without spiritual legitimacy and moral grounding degenerates into abusive despotism.
Military strength always overrides spiritual taboos without consequence.
Priests should be executed whenever the treasury is empty.
questions.explanation: The play shows that authority detached from moral grounding and ancestral taboos quickly becomes abusive.

questions.text: What is the primary function of Iya Agba's character in advancing the plot?
options: She provides comedic interludes between battles.
She reveals hidden truths, dispenses spiritual remedies, and directs the counter-ritual that undoes the tyrant.
She manages the king's palace treasury.
She serves as Chief Serubawon's defense lawyer.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba is the linchpin of resolution: she unmasks past lies, heals the victim, and orchestrates the tyrant's defeat.

questions.text: Which theme is most prominently explored through the plight of Omoyeni and Desola?
options: The advantages of arranged marriages
The exploitation, violation, and commodification of women under authoritarian patriarchy
The unimportance of romance in traditional society
The economic benefits of royal polygamy
questions.explanation: Their suffering lays bare the vulnerability of women under patriarchal and autocratic systems that treat people as property.

questions.text: What does the resolution of the play imply about the nature of justice in human society?
options: Justice is an illusion that never occurs in mortal affairs.
Justice requires moral courage, speaking truth to power, and the courage to challenge institutional corruption.
Justice can only be enforced by foreign colonial authorities.
The wicked always triumph over the righteous in the end.
questions.explanation: The play demonstrates that justice is active, requiring collective courage and principled action to triumph over wrong.

questions.text: How does the play critique the contemporary phenomenon of African 'sit-tight' rulers?
options: By praising leaders who rule for fifty years without elections
By allegorizing the obsession with perpetual power through Ajanaku's desperate, monstrous quest for immortality
By showing that old leaders are always superior to youth
By arguing that constitutions should be abolished
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's desperate ritual quest for immortality mirrors modern sit-tight rulers who subvert institutions to hold power forever.

questions.text: What role does the theme of hubris play in classical tragedy as reflected in Ajanaku's character?
options: It allows the protagonist to escape divine judgment.
It blinds the flawed leader to his vulnerability, leading him to overstep cosmic bounds and engineer his own doom.
It makes the character beloved by his subjects.
It causes him to surrender his throne to the elders.
questions.explanation: Hubris blinds the leader to reality, leading him to cross sacred boundaries and seal his own destruction.

questions.text: In literature examination terminology, what represents the inciting incident of the play?
options: The marriage of Delani and Omoyeni
The mysterious incapacitation of Oba Akinjobi and Serubawon's plotting to enthrone Olaniyonu
The suicide of Chief Serubawon
The execution of the counter-ritual at the Jobele festival
questions.explanation: The king's illness and Serubawon's plot to install Olaniyonu trigger the entire chain of dramatic events.

questions.text: What is the climax of 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: Chief Odejimi refusing to attend the coronation
The dramatic confrontation at the Jobele festival where Desola embraces Ajanaku and Odekunle binds him with the red cloth
The first meeting between Desola and Odekunle on the bush path
Iya Agba leaving the palace in Scene 3
questions.explanation: The climax occurs at the Jobele festival when the counter-ritual is executed in front of the assembled town.

questions.text: What constitutes the denouement (falling action and resolution) of the drama?
options: Ajanaku defeating the hunters' guild in battle
The collapse of Ajanaku, Serubawon's suicide, Desola's healing, the reunion of the lovers, and the cleansing of the realm
The coronation of Chief Ajasa as the new monarch
The permanent exile of all women from the town
questions.explanation: The denouement untangles every plot thread: the tyrant falls, the architect dies, the victims heal, and order returns.

questions.text: How is poetic justice demonstrated in the fate of Chief Serubawon?
options: He is rewarded with double lands by the recovering king.
The very monster he birthed and crowned violates his beloved daughter, forcing him to face the bitter fruit of his ambition.
He escapes to an adjacent town with the palace gold.
He is named the new high priest of Ogun.
questions.explanation: Poetic justice is served when the dark instrument he created destroys his own family, exposing his treachery.

questions.text: What does the contrast between Chief Odejimi and Chief Ajasa reveal about parental duty?
options: Parents should always yield their children to royal demands.
Odejimi protects his son and stands for truth, while Ajasa cowardly sells his daughter's happiness to appease power.
Neither father cares about the welfare of his offspring.
Ajasa is wiser because he avoids conflict with the palace.
questions.explanation: Odejimi defends his family with courage, while Ajasa cowardly trades his daughter's happiness for royal favor.

questions.text: Why is the play particularly relevant for contemporary African civic education?
options: It teaches students how to trap wild game in the savanna.
It critiques autocracy, exposes the perils of sycophancy, champions women's agency, and emphasizes moral accountability.
It advocates for the elimination of traditional ceremonies.
It encourages citizens to submit blindly to military regimes.
questions.explanation: The drama serves as a potent civic critique, challenging autocracy and sycophancy while advocating moral courage.

questions.text: Which character serves as a dramatic foil to King Ajanaku?
options: Chief Serubawon
Chief Odejimi (representing principled restraint and humility over tyrannical hubris)
Chief Ajasa
Odegbami
questions.explanation: Odejimi serves as a moral foil to Ajanaku: humble where the king is arrogant, and principled where the king is rapacious.

questions.text: What does the term 'Ajanaku' symbolize in traditional African political discourse?
options: delicate balance of democratic powers
An overwhelming, unstoppable executive force that crushes dissent like an elephant in the forest
The peaceful trade of agricultural produce
The scholarly pursuit of traditional medicine
questions.explanation: In African political discourse, the elephant symbolizes an overbearing executive power that tramples the grassroots.

questions.text: How does the playwright avoid turning the characters into simplistic two-dimensional caricatures?
options: By having all characters commit identical crimes
By giving conspirators like Serubawon and Demoke genuine human affection for their daughter, making their tragedy poignant.
By eliminating all dialogue between family members
By making the tyrant apologize every morning
questions.explanation: Giving the conspirators genuine parental love for Desola makes their moral complicity and grief profoundly tragic.

questions.text: What role does the setting of the 'Jobele Festival' play in highlighting dramatic irony?
options: It allows the actors to wear foreign costumes.
The public celebrates harvest and joy, unaware that a life-and-death struggle to topple the tyrant is unfolding in their midst.
It prevents the hunters from bringing weapons.
It marks the end of the dry season.
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony shines as the crowd celebrates, oblivious to the high-stakes confrontation about to erupt.

questions.text: What central thesis does Ademilua-Afolayan's 'Once Upon an Elephant' advance regarding power?
