options: Power belongs permanently to whoever possesses the greatest physical ruthlessness.
Power is a sacred trust that, when corrupted by hubris and greed, destroys both the ruler and his co-conspirators.
Monarchs have divine immunity from moral laws.
Injustice can only be cured by foreign military intervention.
questions.explanation: The play's central thesis is that authority is a sacred trust; when twisted into tyranny, it devours ruler and enabler alike.

questions.text: What does the title 'Once Upon an Elephant' signify about the cyclical nature of history?
options: That elephants will always inhabit Nigerian forests
That tyrants rise periodically, but their monstrous reigns are fleeting chapters that eventually come to an end.
That kingdoms must celebrate coronation ceremonies annually
That storytelling is reserved exclusively for children
questions.explanation: The fable title suggests that while tyrants rise periodically, their monstrous rules are ultimately fleeting chapters.

questions.text: Why is the dialogue between Iya Agba and Chief Serubawon in Scene 11 considered the turning point of the play?
options: Serubawon successfully arrests Iya Agba and locks her in the palace.
The buried truth of Ajanaku's paternity and the incestuous nature of the assault are laid bare, breaking Serubawon's resolve.
They agree to divide the kingdom's treasury equally.
Iya Agba begs Serubawon for palace protection.
questions.explanation: Scene 11 breaks the conspiracy wide open: confronting the horror of his deeds shatters Serubawon's will to protect the tyrant.

questions.text: How does the play resolve the tension between ancestral custom and political manipulation?
options: By discarding all traditional customs in favor of foreign laws
By demonstrating that while corrupt leaders manipulate customs for selfish ends, authentic traditions contain the tools to purify society.
By proving that customs are inherently oppressive to all citizens
By crowning a foreign trader as the permanent king
questions.explanation: The play shows that while schemers manipulate custom, true ancestral traditions hold the moral power to heal the community.

questions.text: What is the thematic significance of Desola being an only child?
options: It reduces the financial burden on Serubawon's household.
It heightens the tragedy of her violation, striking directly at the continuation of Serubawon's family lineage.
It makes her ineligible for traditional marriage.
It forces her to become a hunter.
questions.explanation: As an only child, Desola represents the entire future of her lineage; her violation strikes at the heart of Serubawon's legacy.

questions.text: How does the playwright depict the moral evolution of Demoke?
options: She remains an unrepentant conspirator until the very end.
Her daughter's suffering shatters her arrogance, transforming her from a palace schemer into a weeping, repentant mother.
She poisons Serubawon to seize his chieftaincy title.
She joins Ajanaku's palace guards.
questions.explanation: Witnessing her daughter's torment breaks Demoke's pride, turning her from a ruthless schemer into a remorseful mother.

questions.text: What does the character of Odegbami contribute to the thematic representation of the Hunters' Guild?
options: He shows that hunters are easily bought with royal gifts.
He represents the guild's loyalty to the land and customary order, serving as a pillar of martial resistance against despotism.
He advises the hunters to abandon the kingdom.
He acts as King Ajanaku's personal executioner.
questions.explanation: Odegbami embodies the hunters' integrity, demonstrating that true warriors defend the people, not tyrannical crowns.

questions.text: Why is the counter-ritual executed through a young woman (Desola) and a young hunter (Odekunle)?
options: The elder chiefs were too frail to attend the festival.
It symbolizes the youth reclaiming their stolen future and leading the physical and spiritual renewal of the land.
King Ajanaku refused to speak to older citizens.
The traditional laws prohibited elders from wearing red cloth.
questions.explanation: Empowering Desola and Odekunle emphasizes the youth rising to reclaim their stolen future and restore the land.

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the danger of remaining silent during early signs of injustice?
options: Silence is the safest path to personal prosperity.
Silence in the face of overreach allows corruption to take root until it grows into an unstoppable monster that devours all.
Rulers respect silent subjects more than those who speak.
Silence ensures that taxes remain low.
questions.explanation: The play shows that early complacency allows small abuses to mushroom into monstrous tyranny.

questions.text: How is the communal concept of 'Ajo' (collective assembly and solidarity) demonstrated in the resolution?
options: The townspeople scatter into different forests.
All segments—elders, youth, women, hunters—unite to purge the abomination and celebrate collective liberation.
The assembly votes to abolish traditional kingship forever.
The townspeople hand the kingdom over to an invading army.
questions.explanation: True renewal is realized when all strata of society unite to purge the rot and rebuild communal life.

questions.text: What does the playwright imply regarding the role of memory and oral history in society?
options: Historical memory is useless and should be forgotten.
Preserving historical truth (as embodied by Iya Agba) prevents the erasure of justice and arms the community against deceit.
History should only be recorded by the ruling monarch.
Oral memories should be replaced by foreign decrees.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba proves that remembering historical truth protects a society from falling prey to revisionist lies.

questions.text: Why does King Ajanaku mock the warnings of the ancestors?
options: He was educated in a foreign country that rejected religion.
His intoxicating arrogance and belief in his ritual invulnerability made him view himself as superior to the gods.
The ancestral priests had officially crowned him as a god.
He knew the ancestors were fictional characters.
questions.explanation: Blinded by megalomania and ritual dark power, Ajanaku foolishly considers himself beyond ancestral reckoning.

questions.text: What is the symbolic function of the unmasked truth in dismantling Ajanaku's power?
options: It allows the British court to intervene.
Tyranny thrives on secrecy and deceit; speaking unadorned truth dissolves the psychological illusion of the despot's invincibility.
It convinces Ajanaku to give up his personal wealth.
It causes the palace walls to collapse physically.
questions.explanation: Autocracy relies on secrecy and terror; bringing unvarnished truth to light shatters the illusion of invulnerability.

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of legitimate vs. illegitimate succession?
options: Any individual who seizes power by force is fully legitimate.
Legitimate rule requires adherence to customary vetted protocols, moral rectitude, and the genuine consensus of the governed.
Legitimacy is determined strictly by the number of soldiers a ruler commands.
Succession should be decided by wrestling matches.
questions.explanation: Legitimate governance demands constitutional protocols, moral integrity, and the genuine consent of the governed.

questions.text: What does Omoyeni's pregnancy symbolize in the larger narrative arc?
options: The continuation of King Ajanaku's royal line
The persistence of innocent life, hope, and love outlasting the oppressive darkness of the palace.
The inevitable triumph of royal polygamy
financial burden on Chief Ajasa's household
questions.explanation: Her pregnancy represents life, endurance, and hope persevering despite the oppressive darkness of the palace.

questions.text: How does Chief Odejimi's household function as a thematic sanctuary in the drama?
options: It is built with iron walls that arrows cannot penetrate.
It represents an unwavering sanctuary of ethical truth, mutual respect, and fidelity where conscience is never compromised.
It is where all the kingdom's tax revenues are stored.
It provides shelter for foreign mercenaries.
questions.explanation: Odejimi's home stands as an ethical lighthouse, modeling moral clarity in a sea of societal compromise.

questions.text: What does the collapse of King Ajanaku teach students about the limitations of physical might?
options: Physical strength is the only attribute that endures in human affairs.
Brute physical power and political coercion are inherently fragile when confronted by moral truth and cosmic justice.
Hunters should always avoid wrestling with kings.
Only weapons made of bronze can defeat autocrats.
questions.explanation: The play shows that physical force is brittle; when confronted by truth and united will, autocracy collapses.

questions.text: In what way is 'Once Upon an Elephant' a cautionary tale for modern African political elites?
options: It warns elites to build stronger palace prisons for their critics.
It warns that exploiting national institutions, abusing the vulnerable, and subverting justice will inevitably trigger ruinous reckoning.
It advises leaders to ban all traditional harvest festivals.
It suggests that leaders should rely exclusively on foreign loans.
questions.explanation: The drama warns that trampling institutions and exploiting citizens produces a reckoning no elite can escape.

questions.text: Why is the healing of Desola central to the play's moral resolution?
options: It allows her father Serubawon to reclaim his chieftaincy post.
It confirms that the counter-ritual was successful, restoring not only the political order but also the physical and spiritual victims of tyranny.
It enables her to become the next queen mother.
It proves that European medicines are unnecessary in the village.
questions.explanation: Her restoration confirms the spiritual victory, showing that justice must heal the wounded, not merely punish the guilty.

questions.text: Which dramatic movement characterizes the final scenes of the play?
options: descent into cynical nihilism and hopeless civil war
triumphant catharsis combining ritual purification, justice, romantic reunion, and communal renewal
An abrupt, unexplained cliffhanger leaving all fates unresolved
silent transition into modern prose narration
questions.explanation: The play ends in radiant catharsis, harmonizing justice, ritual cleansing, romance, and communal rebirth.

questions.text: What is the ultimate literary achievement of Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan in 'Once Upon an Elephant'?
options: She wrote a simple folktale intended exclusively for primary school children.
She successfully fused indigenous oral performance traditions, Yoruba mythology, and biting political satire to create a masterpiece on the tragedy of tyranny.
She translated classical Greek drama into modern English without African references.
She documented the colonial history of big-game hunting in West Africa.
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan's achievement lies in blending indigenous oral theatre, myth, and satire into a timeless critique of power.
